title: Does the ratio of two ages stay the same as years pass?
description: When Ziva was three, the mother was ten times as old. The video finds the ratio of their ages then and nine years later, and compares the two ratios by cross multiplying. Keeko doubts that the ratio changes and thinks it stays one to ten.
teaching_notes: One idea: adding the same number of years to both terms changes a ratio, so the new ratio is not in proportion with the old one. Watch for students who keep the ratio at one to ten and multiply the new age by ten.

source: Ziva is 3 and the mother is 10 times as old. What is the
video_script.why: The child sees that years are added to both ages, not multiplied, so the ratio of the ages is not kept.
video_script.substitution: Write the ratio now, add the same years to both ages, write the new ratio, and compare the two by cross multiplying.
video_script.anchor: the girl and her mother whose ages are compared at three years and at twelve years, from the book
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko keeps the ratio at one to ten and multiplies the new age of twelve by ten, which treats the nine added years as if they were multiplied.
video_script.payoff_line: The ratio changes from one to ten to four to thirteen

final_answer.value: 1 : 10 now and 4 : 13 at age 12; the ratio changes
final_answer.spoken: one to ten at first and four to thirteen later, so the ratio changes

names.Ziva: the girl whose age and whose mother's age show that adding years changes a ratio

never_show: 1 : 10 kept at age 12, marked as right
maths_rules: mother's age at 3: 3 × 10 = 30; ratio 3 : 30 = 1 : 10 (divide both by 3)
cross multiplying 1 : 10 and 4 : 13: 1 × 13 = 13 and 10 × 4 = 40, not equal
Keeko's slip: 12 × 10 = 120, but the mother is 39
video_script.design: One idea: the same years added to both ages change the ratio. The two ages sit as bars on the stage, with the ratio on the board, and Keeko's one hundred twenty is struck at the end.

marks.ratio: 3 : 30 = 1 : 10 is written with both terms divided by 3

narration: <bookmark mark='mother'/>Step one, the mother was three times ten, which is thirty.
<bookmark mark='ratio'/>The ratio of their ages was three to thirty, which is one to ten in its simplest form.
<bookmark mark='years'/>Step two, Ziva turns twelve after nine more years.
<bookmark mark='mother'/>In those nine years, the mother also grows older by nine, so the mother is thirty nine.

marks.simp: 12 : 39 = 4 : 13 is written with both terms divided by 3

narration: <bookmark mark='new'/>Step three, the new ratio is twelve to thirty nine.
<bookmark mark='simp'/>The highest common factor is three, so dividing both terms by three gives four to thirteen.

marks.cross: 1 × 13 = 13 and 10 × 4 = 40 are written with a not-equal sign between them

narration: <bookmark mark='cross'/>Step four, compare the two ratios by cross multiplying. One times thirteen is thirteen. Ten times four is forty. The two are not equal.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 1 : 10 now and 4 : 13 at age 12; the ratio changes

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The ratio changes from one to ten to four to thirteen.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows 12 × 10 = 120; a tall bar of 120 blocks appears beside the bar of 39; the bubble is struck through and the bars show 30 + 9 = 39

marks.bars: a tall bar of 120 blocks appears next to the bar of 39
marks.fix: the bubble is struck through and 30 + 9 = 39 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the ratio stays one to ten, so the mother would be one hundred twenty.
<bookmark mark='bars'/>But the mother lived only nine more years, not ninety more.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Both ages grew by adding years, not by multiplying, so the ratio could not stay the same.
